analysis.one_liner: Extends child labor protections to independent-contractor kids and sharply raises penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Stop Child Labor Act never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a loophole in federal child labor law: companies that classify children as independent contractors instead of employees would no longer escape the rules. It would also raise civil fines for child labor violations, with steep fines for repeat or willful violators, add prison time for repeated violations, create a grant program to help employers prevent violations, and stand up an advisory committee on child labor. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers working in the United States, including those currently classified as independent contractors, who would gain new protections and the ability to sue employers who harm them. Working families benefit when their kids are kept out of hazardous work.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Fair Labor Standards Act's child labor rules to independent contractors, closing a gap that currently lets companies avoid child labor rules by classifying children as contractors rather than employees.

Raises civil fines for child labor violations from a maximum of $11,000 per violation to a range of $5,000 to $132,270, and for repeat or willful violations from a $50,000 maximum to a range of $25,000 to $601,150, with both amounts automatically increasing each year with inflation.
Makes repeated or willful child labor violations a crime punishable by a fine of up to $50,000, up to one year in prison, or both — the first criminal penalty tied to this specific violation.
Lets a child harmed by a child labor violation sue the employer for compensatory and punitive damages of up to $250,000, a private enforcement tool that currently does not exist for this violation.
Creates a grant program, funded through nonprofits, employer associations, and labor organizations, to educate and train employers to recognize and prevent child labor violations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who use child labor, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, food processing, construction, and delivery services, would face far higher fines, possible criminal prosecution, and lawsuits from harmed children. Compliant employers would bear modest costs from grant-funded training and compliance activity.

drawbacks.text: The new minimum civil penalty of $5,000 applies even to minor or first-time violations, and punitive damages up to $250,000 per child could expose small businesses and family operations to expensive litigation over ordinary mistakes.

The bill does not add new inspectors or funding for wage-and-hour enforcement, so steeper penalties on paper only deter violations if the Labor Department actually investigates, which it may not do at current staffing levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — closing the independent-contractor loophole and making violations expensive enough to deter them — is significant given the rise in reported child labor violations in hazardous work. The costs fall almost entirely on businesses that break the law, though small employers face real exposure from minimum penalties and lawsuits. A reasonable bill would pair the steeper penalties with enforcement funding; this one leaves that gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on October 17, 2023, joined by Republican Sen. Todd Young as an original cosponsor, making it bipartisan from day one.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

No further action appears in the record: the committee never scheduled it for consideration, no version was reported out, and the full Senate and House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that employ or benefit from child labor, especially where children are misclassified as independent contractors, keep operating under the old rules with low maximum fines of $11,000 per violation and no criminal exposure for repeat violations. Children in hazardous work got no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers relying on the old child labor rules

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Child Labor Act on October 17, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Todd Young
for.role: Original cosponsor, U.S. Senator from Indiana
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction, giving it Republican support from day one.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in origin — a Democrat sponsoring with one of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsoring — and no one voted against it or recorded opposition; it simply never advanced.

industries.note: Agriculture is the largest user of legal child farm labor and has a long history of violations; higher penalties and child lawsuits raise the cost of breaking the rules. Children working in agriculture stand to gain protections they largely lack today.

Cleaning contractors in meatpacking plants have been prominent offenders in recent federal child labor cases; the bill's higher fines, criminal exposure for repeat violations, and independent-contractor coverage directly target how these violations are structured.

Hazardous construction work by minors is a recurring violation area, and much of it uses subcontracted labor; extending the law to independent contractors removes that shield and adds lawsuit exposure.

Platforms that route work through independent contractors, including minors, would become directly liable under child labor rules for the first time, while compliant operations face mainly compliance costs.
